Story A explicitly accounts for every odd detail, including the officer's approving nod, his wait at the gate until noon, and her lingering thirst. Story B explains the dilution mechanism well but leaves the nod and the noon wait less directly addressed.
rounds.fact:
REAL

WADA's International Standard for Testing and Investigations requires a sample to have a specific gravity of at least 1.005 (by refractometer) or be rejected as unsuitable, so the Doping Control Officer must collect additional samples until one meets the requirement, and athletes are advised not to over-hydrate. The 60-minute whereabouts window for out-of-competition testing is also real.

rounds.riddle: For fifteen days in Ryogoku he never once stepped into the ring, though his name sat printed on the ranking sheet. His doctor said to quit in spring, but he held on for one more sheet. Months later the ring was his, and a man with scissors waited until last as hundreds applauded.
rounds.chars: An injured juryo wrestler, 29 tournaments into his career as a salaried sekitori; his stable's topknot hairdresser (tokoyama)
rounds.story: The wrestler was one tournament short of the 30 sekitori tournaments the Sumo Association requires before it will hold a full topknot-cutting ceremony in the Kokugikan ring. Because that count is based on appearing on the banzuke ranking sheet rather than on bouts fought, and an absence only lowers his rank on the next sheet, he sat out the whole summer tournament while still listed, retired afterward, and later had the final snip made by his hairdresser after the guests had each cut a strand.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Takeshi, an injured veteran sumo wrestler.

**Character 2:** His stablemaster (oyakata), a former yokozuna who now trains wrestlers.

**Story:** Ignoring his doctor's spring advice to retire, Takeshi sat out the entire fifteen-day Ryogoku tournament injured, just to keep his name on one more ranking sheet and reach the rank or service time he needed for a formal retirement ceremony and an elder's licence. Months later the Kokugikan ring was his alone for that ceremony, where hundreds of guests each snipped his topknot while his stablemaster waited with the scissors to make the final cut.
rounds.judge:
B

Story B explains precisely why one more ranking sheet mattered: sumo's 30-tournament threshold for a ring ceremony counts listings rather than bouts, so sitting out still counted. Story A only gestures vaguely at "rank or service time."
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

The Sumo Association's rule for a full danpatsu-shiki in the ring is generally 30 tournaments as a sekitori, but that count is based on tournaments in which the wrestler actually competed as sekitori (not merely appearing on the banzuke), and the claim that sitting out while still ranked counts is not how it works. Also, the final snip is traditionally made by the wrestler's stablemaster (oyakata), not the hairdresser, though the tokoyama does tidy the hair afterward.

Actually, the rule is commonly described as 30 tournaments as sekitori (including those ranked but absent), and the final cut is by the stablemaster, so the answer's details are partly wrong; the scenario's central mechanism is thus materially off.

rounds.riddle:
On a rig outside Odessa, the new hand griped all morning about a rotten-egg stink, and the old man just kept drilling.
At noon the new hand grinned and said the smell was finally gone.
The old man went white, ordered the well shut in, and sent the bearded new hand alone up the hill, into the wind.
The clean-shaven men stayed behind.
rounds.chars: Cody, a bearded new roughneck; Earl (toolpusher)
rounds.story: The well had drilled into a Permian sour-gas zone, and Earl tolerated the rotten-egg smell because hydrogen sulfide at a few parts per million is only a nuisance. Near 100 ppm, though, the gas paralyzes the olfactory nerve, so Cody's "the smell is gone" meant the concentration had climbed toward lethal, and because H2S is heavier than air and pools in low ground, and a breathing-apparatus facepiece cannot seal over a beard (OSHA 1910.134), Earl sent Cody uphill and upwind while the shaved crew masked up and stayed to shut in the well.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Hank, the bearded new hand (a roughneck on his first week)

**Character 2:** Earl, the old driller (a veteran oilfield drilling foreman)

**Story:** Hank's "finally gone" meant the hydrogen sulfide (sour gas) had climbed to a level that paralyzes the sense of smell, so the stink vanishing was a sign of deadly concentration, not safety. Earl shut in the well and sent Hank uphill and upwind, since the heavy gas pools low, while the clean-shaven crew stayed behind to fight the leak in breathing masks that would never seal over Hank's beard.
rounds.judge:
B

Story B accounts for every detail, including why the old man kept drilling through the early stink (low-ppm H2S is only a nuisance), which Story A leaves unexplained.
rounds.fact:
REAL

H2S causes olfactory fatigue at high concentrations (around 100 ppm), is heavier than air and pools in low areas, and OSHA 1910.134 prohibits facial hair that interferes with a respirator's seal, so the scenario's mechanisms are accurate.

rounds.riddle:
Summer 1943: a stopped tanker sat broadside to the submarine, the textbook shot every captain dreams of.
The torpedoman begged his captain to move the boat and fire from a sloppy, glancing angle instead.
The captain refused, and eleven fish struck the hull squarely without a single fire.
The torpedoman then guarded the last one like treasure and refused to fire it, and the admirals later thanked him for it.
rounds.chars: Commander Dan Daspit; Chief Ray Kowalski (torpedoman's mate)
rounds.story: Daspit's crew aboard USS Tinosa carried Mark 14 torpedoes, which had a notorious contact-exploder defect, so their hits on the crippled Tonan Maru No. 3 kept producing duds, and Kowalski had noticed that the boat's earlier hits from oblique angles had exploded. The lesser-known consequence was this: a clean 90-degree impact decelerated the warhead so violently that the exploder's firing pin bent or jammed on its guide before it reached the cap, while glancing hits slowed the torpedo gently enough to fire, so the perfect broadside shot was the worst possible one, and Kowalski saved the last torpedo so it could be taken back to Pearl Harbor, where drop tests on it proved the flaw and led to a redesigned firing pin.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Lt. Cmdr. Dan Daspit, captain of USS *Tinosa*

**Character 2:** The boat's chief torpedoman (occupation: torpedoman, the sailor who maintains and fires the sub's torpedoes)

**Story:** The torpedoman knew the Mark 6 exploder's secret flaw: a square, 90-degree hit crushed the firing pin before it could detonate, so only glancing hits like the ones that had first stopped the *Tonan Maru No. 3* actually exploded. Daspit kept firing "perfect" shots that clanged off the hull as duds, so the torpedoman saved the last fish and brought it home to Pearl Harbor, where it became the evidence that forced the admirals to fix the torpedo.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A explains every detail more completely: the tanker was already crippled by earlier oblique hits, a square impact jammed the firing pin while glancing hits fired, and the saved torpedo was tested at Pearl Harbor and led to a redesigned firing pin, which accounts for the admirals' gratitude.
rounds.fact: REAL. The Mark 14's contact exploder did fail on near-perpendicular hits because the firing pin was slowed or jammed by the violent deceleration, while glancing hits often worked. Tinosa's July 1943 attack on Tonan Maru No. 3 produced duds, and Dan Daspit saved a last torpedo, which was tested at Pearl Harbor and proved the flaw, though the exact details of Kowalski's role and the "redesigned firing pin" are somewhat embellished.

rounds.riddle: Off Iceland, the trawler hauled in nothing but a sealed crate, and the skipper wept with relief. He radioed ashore at once, then ordered the nets cut loose and the engine stopped. The man who came aboard at dawn gave the crate one glance, ignored the skipper's offered coffee, and wrote down only the time.
rounds.chars: Skipper Gunnar, a trawler captain; Halla, a customs officer
rounds.story: Gunnar's trawler, fishing illegally inside a newly extended fishery limit, had been dodging the coast guard, and when he snagged a crate of contraband he realized he had a way out: under Icelandic law, he reasoned, a vessel that reports salvage of wreck or cargo and stops immediately is a vessel in distress or salvage, not poaching, so he radioed in and cut his nets loose, which ended his illegal catch. Halla, the customs officer, wrote down only the time because the salvage clause says that the finder's reporting time, not the discovery time, fixes the salvage claim and the legal point at which the vessel's position was logged; by stopping the engine and reporting immediately, Gunnar's logged time proved he was inside the limit only because of salvage, so his fishing-ban violation was voided while he still claimed his reward.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Skipper Gunnar, a trawler captain whose brother vanished at sea in those waters weeks earlier.

**Character 2:** Lieutenant Sigrún, a navy bomb-disposal officer.

**Story:** Gunnar had dreaded every haul since his brother's boat disappeared, so when the nets brought up a sealed crate instead of a body he wept with relief. But the crate was stamped as a WWII timed demolition charge, so he radioed the coast guard, cut the nets and stopped the engine to avoid jolting it, and at dawn Sigrún took one glance, refused the coffee because there was no time, and wrote down the hour her team would detonate it.
rounds.judge:
B
Story B naturally explains the weeping (relief that the haul wasn't his brother's body), the cut nets and stopped engine (to avoid jolting the explosive), and the glance, refused coffee and recorded time (an urgent bomb-disposal assessment), whereas Story A depends on a contrived legal loophole and leaves the weeping and refused coffee unexplained.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
No known Icelandic or international salvage law voids a fishing-limit violation because a vessel reports found cargo and stops, nor does a salvage clause make the reporting time fix a legal position log in that way.

rounds.riddle:
For a wedding in Thrissur with no priest, no muhurtham and exactly three witnesses, Anil and Fathima flew home together from Dubai.
Her family stopped speaking to her the day both their names appeared on an office noticeboard.
Everyone knows that paper must hang for thirty days, yet Anil had begged his boss for sixty-one days' leave.
He married on the very last of them.
rounds.chars: Anil, a Dubai-based groom; Mr. Raghavan (sub-registrar and marriage officer)
rounds.story: Anil is Hindu and Fathima is Muslim, so they could only marry before sub-registrar Raghavan under the Special Marriage Act, 1954, which requires three witnesses and a public notice on his office board; that notice is how her family found out. The famous 30-day objection period was only half the wait: Section 5 of the Act lets Raghavan accept the notice only after one party has lived in his district for 30 days, so the Dubai residents had to stay in Thrissur for a month before filing, then wait out the 30 days, and could marry on day 61.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Fathima, Anil's Muslim fiancée.
**Character 2:** Anil, a Hindu site engineer working in Dubai.

**Story:** Because their interfaith marriage had to happen under India's Special Marriage Act, Anil first had to live in Thrissur for 30 days before he could file a notice with the Marriage Officer, and that notice then had to hang publicly on the office noticeboard for another 30 days. Fathima's family saw their names posted there and cut her off, but on day 61 of his leave the couple finally signed the register at the office before the three legally required witnesses, with no priest and no auspicious hour.
rounds.judge:
A

Story A covers every odd detail, including the absence of a priest and muhurtham, the family cutting her off, and signing on day 61, while Story B gives the same residency-plus-notice explanation without addressing the missing priest and auspicious hour.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

Under the Special Marriage Act, 1954, Section 5 requires notice to the Marriage Officer of a district where at least one party has resided for 30 days, and Section 7 gives a 30-day objection period after publication, so the two periods do exist. However, the residency requirement means one party must live there for 30 days before the notice is given, and the notice may be filed on day 31 rather than after a month of waiting, which makes "day 61" roughly plausible. The more serious problem is the claim that three witnesses and the notice board are how the family found out, and the claim that the residency is a mandatory "wait" for both. The notice is indeed displayed in the office, and three witnesses are required at solemnization (Section 12). Nothing in the mechanism is truly invented, so the label should be REAL.

REAL

The Special Marriage Act does require 30 days' residence in the district before notice (Section 5), a 30-day public notice/objection period (Sections 7 and 8), and three witnesses at the solemnization, so the mechanism works roughly as described.

rounds.riddle:
Grandfather laid down a cask at a Speyside distillery the day she was born, to be opened on her fiftieth birthday.
At forty-seven the distillery's man phoned: "Bottle it this month, or it stops being whisky."
"There's plenty left," he added, "and nothing's spoiled. It's simply been too patient in our damp Scottish air."
So she bottled early, and her label reads "47 Years Old," three years short of the promise.
rounds.chars: Morag Grant, the granddaughter; Callum Reid (distillery warehouse manager)
rounds.story: Callum's routine hydrometer check showed the cask had slipped from its original 63.5% to 40.3% ABV, because in a cool, humid Scottish dunnage warehouse alcohol evaporates out through the oak faster than water does, so the angels' share lowers a cask's strength rather than just its volume. Under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009, spirit below 40% ABV can never legally be sold as Scotch whisky, and nothing but water or caramel may be added to it, so it cannot be fortified back up. Waiting three more years would have turned Grandfather's gift into unnamed "spirit drink," and Morag chose a true 47-year-old Scotch over a 50-year-old nothing.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** The granddaughter, now forty-seven, who owns the cask her grandfather laid down at her birth.

**Character 2:** The distillery's warehouse manager, who checks the strength of every cask.

**Story:** In Speyside's damp warehouses, the "angel's share" that evaporates each year is mostly alcohol rather than water, so after forty-seven years her cask still held plenty of liquid, but its strength had sunk to just above 40% ABV, the legal minimum for anything called Scotch whisky. The manager warned that one more summer would take it below 40% for good, so she bottled it that month to freeze it at 47 years, since whisky stops aging once it leaves the cask.
rounds.judge:
A

Story A more fully explains why early bottling was the only option: under the Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 the spirit cannot be fortified back above 40%, a point Story B omits.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

The Scotch Whisky Regulations 2009 do set 40% ABV as the minimum bottling strength, and casks can lose strength to evaporation in humid warehouses. But the account is materially wrong: adding or blending other Scotch whisky into the cask would not be forbidden, and a cask that has fallen below 40% can still be sold as Scotch whisky. Only bottling and retail sale as Scotch requires 40% minimum. Also, the claim that nothing but water or caramel may be added is not a bar to fortifying with other whisky, and the "never legally sold" framing is wrong. The mechanism of evaporation lowering ABV is real, but the legal dead end is overstated, and the 63.5%-to-40.3% drop is plausible but the story's constraint that it "cannot be fortified" is wrong.

rounds.riddle: At the Iten training camp, the night before the Eldoret marathon, the pacer's bib sat folded in a drawer while the favorite's was pinned on at midnight. By dawn the favorite had told no one but had quietly mailed his passport to Nairobi, and the pacer ran the first thirty kilometers with a bib bearing someone else's name. Afterward the pacer was paid in full though he finished nowhere, and the favorite's shoes were never seen on the course.
rounds.chars: Kiprop, a marathon favorite with a hamstring injury; Wanjiru, a race-pacing agent (the pacer's manager and contract negotiator)
rounds.story: Kiprop secretly pulled out the night before with a torn hamstring, so Wanjiru put the pacer in Kiprop's bib to hide the withdrawal from rival camps and keep the race's appearance-fee deal alive (fact #1). Under the World Athletics rule that an elite's start-fee contract is paid only if the athlete is listed on the start line, the substituted bib let the pacer's agent claim the fee, and because pacers are paid on a "pace-to-distance" clause as soon as they pass 30 km, he was paid in full even though he dropped out and finished nowhere (fact #2); the passport mailed to Nairobi was sent to the agent to file the visa-and-entry paperwork that locks in the start-fee.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Kiprono, the favorite.
**Character 2:** Otieno, a professional pacer (hired rabbit).

**Story:** Kiprono had secretly accepted a far richer invitation to the Berlin Marathon, so at midnight he pinned his own bib onto Otieno's singlet and at dawn mailed his passport to the Nairobi embassy for his visa, still collecting his Eldoret appearance fee by "starting" the race. Otieno ran the first thirty kilometers disguised under Kiprono's name and then stepped off the course, exactly as pacers always do, so he was paid in full. Meanwhile Kiprono's own shoes stayed packed for Germany.
rounds.judge:
B

Story B explains every detail with one simple motive: the favorite secretly chose a richer race abroad, so the passport goes to Nairobi for a visa, his bib goes on the pacer at midnight, and his shoes stay packed. Story A relies on invented rules and gives a weak reason for mailing a passport for a domestic race.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

World Athletics has no rule that pays a start-fee only if the athlete is listed on the start line, and bib substitution to claim the fee isn't a recognized mechanism. Pacer pay is set by individual contract, not a standard "pace-to-distance" clause at 30 km. Bib swapping would also violate identity and entry rules rather than work as a legal payment mechanism.

rounds.riddle:
July 1943, Pacific: a giant tanker lay stopped and broadside-on to the submarine, a textbook shot.
The skipper cursed the perfect angle and crept round to a worse one before firing again.
With the tanker still afloat and one torpedo left, he turned for Pearl Harbor.
There, a man in a workshop thanked him for the one he didn't fire.
rounds.chars: Lt. Cdr. Dan Hollis, submarine skipper; Ed Marsh (torpedo exploder technician at the Pearl Harbor ordnance shop)
rounds.story: Hollis's two hasty skewed shots had exploded and stopped the tanker, but every Mark 14 torpedo he then fired square into her side hit with a thud and failed to detonate, so he suspected the perfect angle itself and brought the last one home as evidence. Marsh's drop tests on it proved him right: the contact exploder's firing pin slides crosswise in guide studs, and the violent deceleration of a square 90-degree hit jams and bends it before it reaches the primer, while a glancing hit slows the torpedo gently enough for the pin to fire, which is why the "worse" angle was the better shot.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Lt. Cdr. Dan Daspit, skipper of USS *Tinosa*

**Character 2:** A torpedo-shop ordnance engineer at Pearl Harbor

**Story:** Daspit hit the stalled tanker *Tonan Maru No. 3* with dud after dud, because the Mark 6 exploder's firing pin was crushed and failed on a perfect 90° impact, so he swung around to oblique angles hoping a glancing blow would fire. He then deliberately carried his last torpedo home intact as evidence, and the engineer who took it apart confirmed the firing-pin flaw that had been sabotaging American submarines for nearly two years.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A covers every odd detail: how the tanker came to be stopped, why the perfect angle failed, and why a glancing hit could fire, all through a clear firing-pin mechanism the shop confirmed with the saved torpedo. Story B leaves the initial stop and the success of the oblique shots unexplained.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED. The Mark 14 torpedo's contact exploder really did fail on near-perpendicular hits because of the firing pin's inertia and friction, and the Mark 6 exploder issues were real, but the specific people and events here are fabricated or conflated, since "Dan Hollis" and "Ed Marsh" don't match the historical record.

Actually, let me reconsider the mechanism itself: the real finding (Mare Island/Pearl Harbor tests, 1943) was that the firing pin in the contact exploder was too slow or got jammed by the abrupt deceleration of a square hit, and glancing hits worked better. Lt. Cdr. Dan Daspit (USS Tinosa's Lt. Cdr. L. R. "Dan" Daspit aside, it was Dudley "Mush" Morton and Charles Momsen's Tonopah test) fired at Tonolei Harbor and Tinosa's Lawrence Daspit brought back a dud in July 1943. The mechanism is real, but the names are wrong.

REAL. The Mark 14's contact exploder firing pin jamming on square 90-degree hits was a documented cause of duds, even though the names and details here are altered.

rounds.riddle:
In the red dust of Kaptagat, a blade bites into the heel of an unrun racing shoe.
An inflamed Achilles demands a thick silicone wedge slipped inside,
Yet he insists three millimeters of virgin foam be ground from the outer sole.
A dial caliper confirms the depth, ensuring the final number never exceeds forty.
rounds.chars: Kipchumba; a cobbler
rounds.story: Preparing to leave camp for an upcoming marathon, Kipchumba needed to run with an orthopedic heel lift for his tendinitis without breaching World Athletics' 40-millimeter sole-thickness limit. Because World Athletics Shoe Regulation 5.2 explicitly dictates that the stack height measurement includes any internal orthotic insert, the cobbler had to shave three millimeters off the pristine shoe's exterior outsole so the modified heel would pass pre-race scrutineering.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Kipchoge-style elite Kenyan marathoner, nursing an inflamed Achilles before a major road race.

**Character 2:** A cobbler (shoe technician) in Kaptagat.

**Story:** The runner's physio ordered a silicone heel wedge to ease his Achilles, but World Athletics rules cap road-racing shoe stack height at 40 mm, and the insert counts toward that total. So the cobbler shaved three millimetres of foam off the outsole of the brand-new shoe and checked it with a caliper, keeping the shoe legal so his record wouldn't be disqualified.
rounds.judge:
B

Story B accounts for every riddle detail, including the brand-new shoe, the silicone wedge counting toward the 40 mm limit, the three millimetres shaved, and the caliper check, while Story A never explains the caliper.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
World Athletics' 40 mm limit is real for road racing shoes, but the rules measure the sole thickness and are not described as "Regulation 5.2" including an orthotic insert in that way. In fact, the rules allow medically required customized shoes with approval, and the scenario of shaving the outsole to compensate is not a recognized mechanism.

rounds.riddle:
Every 59 days a rig rolls onto the same dry hole outside Midland, Texas, turns its bit for one afternoon, and hauls off.
The man paying for it has never expected a drop of oil from that hole.
The rancher at the fence counts the days on a calendar and curses each time the bit starts turning.
He'd be a far richer man if the rig showed up just two days late.
rounds.chars: Dale Hobbs, the rancher who owns the land and minerals; Ray Kessler (independent oil operator)
rounds.story: Kessler holds an old, cheap oil lease on Hobbs's ranch that is past its primary term with no production, while a shale boom next door means Hobbs could re-lease the acreage to a major for millions the moment Kessler's lease dies. The lease's standard continuous-operations clause keeps it alive without any oil so long as no more than 60 days pass between drilling or reworking operations, so Kessler sends a rig to scratch at the dry hole on day 59 every time, holding the lease until he can flip it himself while Hobbs counts toward a 61st day that never comes.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Earl, a Midland rancher who owns the mineral rights under his land.

**Character 2:** Victor, an oil company landman (lease speculator) holding Earl's old drilling lease.

**Story:** Earl's lease has a continuous-operations clause: it dies if no drilling happens for 60 days, and a new oil boom means other companies would pay him a fortune in bonus and higher royalties to re-lease his land. So Victor sends a rig every 59 days to spin a bit in a dry hole for one afternoon, keeping the cheap lease legally alive while he waits to flip it, and Earl curses each time, knowing a two-day delay would set him free and make him rich.
rounds.judge:
B
Story B explains why the lease needs operations to survive (it is past its primary term with no production) and ties "two days late" exactly to the 61st day under the 60-day clause, so its account is slightly more complete and precise than A's.
rounds.fact:
REAL
Oil and gas leases commonly include continuous-operations (cessation-of-production/drilling) clauses that keep a lease alive past its primary term if operations recur within a set interval, often 60 to 90 days, though courts may reject sham or non-good-faith operations meant solely to hold the lease.

rounds.riddle:
Paris, March 2023: all through the strike on rue des Martyrs, the queue stayed long and the shelves stayed full, though the ovens were cold and the flour sacks sat unopened.
Each dawn Monsieur Lenoir climbed a ladder and pinned a sheet over exactly one word of his own shop sign.
When a stranger with a notebook stopped to stare from across the street, Lenoir did not hide; he grinned and pointed up at the sheet.
The day his workers came back, the sheet came down before the first loaf was sold.
rounds.chars: Monsieur Lenoir, the shop's owner; Claire Vasseur (consumer-fraud inspector for the DGCCRF)
rounds.story: With his bakers on strike and French labour law forbidding him from hiring temps to replace strikers, Lenoir kept the queue fed with loaves trucked in from an industrial plant, which is why his ovens stayed cold and his flour untouched. Because the 1998 French bakery law reserves the word "boulangerie" on a sign for shops where the dough is kneaded, shaped and baked on the premises, he covered that single word each dawn to avoid a misleading-practice fine, gladly pointed inspector Claire Vasseur to the sheet as proof of compliance, and uncovered it the moment his own bakers were baking again.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Monsieur Lenoir, owner of a bakery on rue des Martyrs.
**Character 2:** A DGCCRF consumer-fraud inspector (the stranger with the notebook).

**Story:** French law says only a shop that kneads and bakes its own bread on site may call itself a "boulangerie." So while his bakers were on strike, Lenoir sold loaves trucked in from a supplier and covered the word "Boulangerie" on his sign every dawn, then grinned at the inspector to show he was fully legal. The morning his workers returned and fired the ovens, the bread was truly his own again, so he uncovered the word before selling the first loaf.
rounds.judge:
A
Both stories share the same core explanation, but A also says why the ovens stayed cold (French law bars hiring temps to replace strikers), so it accounts for the details slightly more completely.
rounds.fact:
REAL

The French 1998 law (Loi du 25 mai 1998, Code de la consommation/Code du commerce art. L121-80ff) does reserve the term "boulangerie" and "boulanger" for businesses that knead, shape, and bake on-site, and violations count as misleading commercial practices enforced by the DGCCRF. French labour law (Code du travail L1242-6) also bars fixed-term or temp contracts to replace striking workers, so the described mechanism is broadly accurate.

rounds.riddle:
Anoop could have flown home from Dubai a fortnight before his Thrissur wedding, but he rebooked for the night before.
He walked through Kochi airport wearing the gold chain meant for his bride's thali.
At the mandapam his mother scolded him for nearly missing his own muhurtham.
He just tapped an old entry stamp in his passport, smiled, and said the wait had paid for itself.
rounds.chars: Meera (bride); Anoop (electrician in Dubai)
rounds.story: Anoop bought Meera's gold thali chain in Dubai and wore it home himself, but he had first landed in Dubai less than a year before his original flight date. India's Baggage Rules allow a male passenger to bring up to 20 g of jewellery duty-free only after living abroad for more than one year, so he pushed his flight back until his passport's old entry stamp was just over a year old, and the chain cleared Kochi customs within his allowance.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Anoop, a groom working in Dubai
**Character 2:** A Kochi airport customs officer

**Story:** Indian rules let a man bring gold jewellery home duty-free only after more than a year abroad, and the old entry stamp showed Anoop had landed in Dubai just under a year before his original flight, so he rebooked to cross the one-year mark. At Kochi the customs officer checked the stamp and waved him through with the thali chain untaxed, saving far more than the scolding cost him.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A explains every detail with a precise mechanism: he wore the chain himself to fit the 20 g personal-jewellery allowance, and he timed his return so his old Dubai entry stamp passed the one-year residency threshold. Story B covers the same ground but is vaguer about why he was wearing the chain.
rounds.fact:
REAL

India's Baggage Rules, 2016 do allow jewellery duty-free up to 20 g (value cap ₹50,000) for a gentleman passenger who has stayed abroad over one year, and 40 g (₹1,00,000) for a lady passenger. The one-year-abroad condition is real, so timing a return around it is plausible.

rounds.riddle: In 1943, a submarine lay silent on the bottom while the enemy's depth charges fell all night. At dawn the cook was ordered to bake bread, and the captain forbade any other cooking for three days. When they surfaced, the cook alone was told to stay below, and every man ashore later swore the bread tasted of nothing.
rounds.chars: A U.S. submarine captain; the boat's cook (a ship's cook, chief commissary steward)
rounds.story: Hidden fact #1: the submarine was crippled and its air was fouling, so the captain wanted to avoid anything that would worsen the atmosphere, and the cook was ordered to bake bread because dough could be made without burning anything while the crew stayed quiet. Hidden fact #2: the cook's galley ovens were electric, and electric ovens draw heavy current from the battery that was needed for survival, but the real reason for the three-day ban is that carbon dioxide absorbent (soda lime) was running out, and baking yeast dough releases CO2 as it rises, so the captain had the cook bake only one batch, fully proofed in the cold, to use the CO2 early while it could still be scrubbed; after surfacing the cook was kept below to scrub and air out the boat, and the bread tasted bland because salt was withheld, since salt-laden food makes men thirsty when fresh water was rationed.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Captain Hale, the submarine's commander.
**Character 2:** Petty Officer Moss, the boat's cook.

**Story:** During the all-night depth-charging, a cracked battery leaked chlorine gas that slowly burned away the crew's sense of smell, so at dawn Hale had Moss bake bread as a test, banning all other cooking so no fumes could mask the gas. Only Moss, who had spent the night breathing flour-dusted air sealed in the galley, could still smell the loaf, so Hale kept him below as the boat's living gas alarm, while the rest of the crew, their noses ruined, swore ashore that the bread had tasted of nothing.
rounds.judge:
A

Story A ties every detail to one cause: chlorine gas destroyed the crew's sense of smell, so the bread served as a smell test, the cooking ban kept fumes from masking the gas, the cook stayed below as a living gas alarm, and the bread tasted of nothing. Story B piles up contradictory, unconnected explanations.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
The scenario is internally incoherent: baking one batch of yeast dough to "use the CO2 early" doesn't reduce the CO2 burden, and withholding salt to curb thirst plus the supposed three-day ban don't form a real procedure, though submarines do ration power, water, and CO2 scrubbers in emergencies.

rounds.riddle:
On a Permian Basin rig, the new hand griped all morning about the rotten-egg stink.
At noon he grinned: "Thank God, it's finally gone."
The man beside him dropped his tongs and sprinted uphill, into the wind.
Only the runner walked off that rig.
rounds.chars: Earl; Ray (driller)
rounds.story: Earl and Ray were drilling into a sour pocket that was leaking hydrogen sulfide, which explains the rotten-egg smell. Ray knew from his H2S safety training that above roughly 100 ppm the gas paralyzes the olfactory nerve, so the smell suddenly vanishing meant the concentration had spiked, and he followed the standard escape procedure of moving upwind and to high ground because H2S is heavier than air, while Earl, reassured, stayed in the pooling gas and collapsed.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Danny, the new hand on his first week.

**Character 2:** Earl, a veteran floorhand and roughneck trained in H2S safety.

**Story:** Danny didn't know that hydrogen sulfide smells like rotten eggs only at low levels, and that a big rise in concentration paralyzes the sense of smell. When he cheered that the stink had "finally gone," Earl knew a lethal gas surge had just knocked out their noses, so he ran upwind and uphill, away from the heavier-than-air gas pooling on the rig floor. Danny took one more breath and collapsed.
rounds.judge:
A

Story A explicitly matches every element: the new hand mistakes his paralyzed sense of smell for the gas clearing, and the veteran beside him recognizes the surge and flees. Story B never establishes who the griping new hand is or who made the remark.
rounds.fact:
REAL
Hydrogen sulfide does cause olfactory fatigue and paralysis at high concentrations (around 100 ppm and above), so the rotten-egg smell vanishes even as the gas becomes more dangerous. H2S is also heavier than air and pools in low areas, so standard safety procedure is to move upwind and to higher ground.

rounds.riddle: At Iten, after the Kaptagat long run, a visitor followed the camp's fastest woman everywhere, even into the latrine, twice. The first time she came out with exactly what was asked for, yet the visitor glanced at its pale colour and shook her head. Then the visitor took away the runner's water bottle, though the girl was parched from thirty kilometres. They sat side by side, the runner thirsty, until dusk.
rounds.chars: Faith Chebet; Grace Wanjiru (doping control officer for the Athletics Integrity Unit)
rounds.story: Wanjiru arrived unannounced to collect an out-of-competition urine sample, so she had to stay with Chebet at all times and watch the sample being passed, which is why she followed her into the latrine twice. Chebet had gulped litres of water after the long run, and under the WADA testing standard a sample must reach a minimum specific gravity (1.005 on a refractometer) even when the volume is sufficient, so the pale, diluted sample was rejected and Wanjiru had to take her water and wait with her until her body produced a concentrated enough one.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Chebet, an elite Kenyan marathoner, the fastest woman at the Iten camp.

**Character 2:** Mrs. Wanjiru, an anti-doping control officer (sample collection chaperone) on a surprise out-of-competition test.

**Story:** Wanjiru had to witness Chebet urinate into the sample cup, but the pale first sample was too dilute (low specific gravity) to be valid for testing. So Wanjiru confiscated Chebet's water bottle, since drinking more would only dilute the next sample, and the two waited together until dusk for a concentrated one.
rounds.judge:
B
Story B accounts for every odd detail more completely: why the visitor entered the latrine twice, why the sample was pale (she had gulped water after the run), and why it was rejected despite being "exactly what was asked for" (enough volume but below the minimum specific gravity).
rounds.fact:
REAL
WADA's International Standard for Testing requires a minimum urine volume (90 mL) and a suitable specific gravity (at least 1.005 by refractometer, or 1.010 by lab-style test strips/other methods), and samples that are too dilute are rejected, so the athlete must stay under continuous observation by the DCO or chaperone until a suitable sample is provided. The direct-observation of voiding and no-advance-notice out-of-competition testing are also genuine procedures.

rounds.riddle:
On an Icelandic trawler, Sigrún's last haul came up a ton heavier than the boat was allowed to bring home.
The skipper didn't dump it or hide it. He had it weighed at the harbour scale under a special code.
The crew earned almost nothing from that ton, and nobody complained.
Ashore, Sigrún's mother, who has never fished, thanked her for it.
rounds.chars: Sigrún, a deckhand; Helga (marine biologist), her mother
rounds.story: Sigrún's final tow brought up cod beyond the trawler's remaining quota, and Icelandic law bans throwing catch back, so the skipper could neither discard it nor land it as normal quota fish. He declared it as "VS-afli", a rule that lets a boat land up to 5% of its catch outside quota, which is then auctioned with only 20% of the value going to the vessel and 80% going to Verkefnasjóður sjávarútvegsins, the fisheries research fund that pays for Helga's cod-stock project.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Sigrún, a deckhand on an Icelandic trawler.

**Character 2:** Her mother, Guðrún, a marine biologist at Iceland's Marine and Freshwater Research Institute, whose research is paid for by the seafood-industry research fund.

**Story:** When Sigrún's last haul came in a ton over quota, the skipper legally landed it under Iceland's "VS-catch" code: the fish is sold at auction, the crew get only a small share, and most of the proceeds go to the fund that finances fisheries research. That fund pays for Guðrún's fish-stock surveys, so the woman who has never cast a net phoned her daughter to thank her for the ton that keeps her lab running.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A covers every odd detail: Iceland's discard ban explains why the skipper didn't dump the ton, and the 20/80 VS split explains why the crew earned almost nothing, which Story B leaves vaguer.
rounds.fact:
REAL

Iceland does ban discarding catch, and "VS-afli" (verðmætisaukning/sjávarútvegs-afli) is a real category allowing vessels to land up to 5% of catch outside their quota, with the proceeds largely (about 80%) going to the Verkefnasjóður sjávarútvegsins and the remainder to the vessel, so the mechanism works roughly as described.

rounds.riddle:
In June 2022, with the hold half empty and the cod still biting, skipper Einar hauled his trawl and raced the Guðrún home to Grindavík, desperate to be moored before Saturday noon.
Yet the year before he had been tied up on the first weekend of June, and this year he fished straight through that Sunday without a worry.
His wife Sólveig, waiting on the quay, never minded his missing that first Sunday: she had been on her feet working all that day herself.
On the Sunday he did make, she was the one who spoke over the wreath for the drowned.
rounds.chars: Einar, skipper of the trawler Guðrún; Sólveig, his wife (Lutheran parish priest)
rounds.story: Einar abandoned good fishing because Iceland's Seamen's Day Act (law 20/1987) requires fishing vessels to be in harbour by noon on the Saturday before Sjómannadagur, the first Sunday in June, so the crew can be ashore for the holiday. The same law says that when that first Sunday is Whitsunday, as it was on 5 June 2022, Seamen's Day moves a week later to 12 June, which is why he could legally fish through the first Sunday while his wife, the parish priest, spent it conducting Pentecost services before leading the seamen's memorial the next week.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Einar, a trawler skipper of the Guðrún.
**Character 2:** Sólveig, his wife, the parish priest of Grindavík.

**Story:** Icelandic law ties up the fishing fleet for Seamen's Day, normally the first Sunday of June, with boats required in port by noon the day before. In 2022, though, Whitsunday fell on 5 June, so Seamen's Day moved to 12 June: Einar fished through Whitsunday while Sólveig led Pentecost services all day, then he raced home the following Saturday to hear her, as priest, bless the memorial wreath for drowned sailors.
rounds.judge:
B

Both stories give the same Seamen's Day/Whitsunday explanation, but B ties every detail to the actual law, which also explains the legal urgency of the Saturday-noon deadline, so it accounts for the riddle a bit more precisely.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED. Iceland's Sjómannadagurinn is held on the first Sunday in June, and when that Sunday is Whitsunday it moves to the following Sunday (this did happen in 2022, when Pentecost fell on 5 June and Seamen's Day was 12 June), but the claim that law 20/1987 requires vessels to be in harbour by noon the Saturday before is not accurate as described, since law 20/1987 is the Seamen's Day law that sets the day itself and does not impose a mandatory harbour-return rule like that.

Reconsidering: the Seamen's Day Act (lög nr. 20/1987, "Lög um sjómannadag") does exist, and it does state that the first Sunday in June is Seamen's Day, moved to the following Sunday if it coincides with Whitsunday. It also provides that fishing vessels shall be in harbour on Seamen's Day, and I recall the harbour obligation covering the day itself, with a Saturday-noon provision being less certain. The core mechanism, a date shift and a harbour requirement, is largely real, and the details are minor embellishment.

REAL

The Seamen's Day law exists, and its Whitsunday shift and harbour-rest requirement work roughly as described.

rounds.riddle: At Kochi airport a mother who never wore gold stepped off the Dubai flight in a heavy chain. Her son, the groom, sat beside her the whole way and wore nothing. At the Guruvayur muhurtham she unclasped it and fastened it on the bride. She never asked for it back.
rounds.chars: Arjun, the groom; Ammini, his mother (nurse in a Dubai hospital)
rounds.story: Ammini wore the bridal chain herself because jewellery worn openly by a returning resident passenger can pass customs duty-free, so the family avoided paying duty on the wedding gold. She, not Arjun, had to wear it because India's Baggage Rules give a woman resident abroad over a year a 40-gram duty-free jewellery allowance, double the 20 grams allowed to a man, so the heavy chain fit within her limit but would have been taxed on him.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Ammini, a widowed mother from Thrissur who never wore gold.

**Character 2:** Rahul, her son, an electrician working in Dubai and the groom.

**Story:** Rahul had saved for two years to buy his bride's wedding chain in Dubai, but Indian customs lets a returning woman bring in far more gold jewellery duty-free than a man, so his mother wore it home on her neck while he sat beside her bare. At the Guruvayur muhurtham Ammini simply fastened it on the bride, because it had never been hers at all; she had only carried it.
rounds.judge:
B

Story B accounts for every odd detail: the gold was the groom's purchase, so it explains why a mother who never wore gold wore it, why the son stayed bare, and why she never asked for it back. Story A explains the customs allowance but leaves her not wearing gold and not asking for it back unaddressed.
rounds.fact: INVENTED. India's Baggage Rules do give higher duty-free jewellery allowances to women than to men (about 40 g for a woman and 20 g for a man, with value caps of ₹1 lakh and ₹50,000), but these apply only to residents who lived abroad over a year, and they cap the jewellery by weight and value. Wearing jewellery openly does not exempt it from duty, so the claim that it passes duty-free simply because it is worn is wrong.

rounds.riddle:
At 5 a.m. a woman Chebet had never met knocked at the Iten camp dormitory, and Chebet let her follow her everywhere, even into the toilet.
Chebet handed her a full cup; the stranger dipped a small instrument in it, shook her head, sealed it anyway, and stayed.
Nobody forbade Chebet anything, yet she skipped the 40 km long run she had been drinking litres of water for, and now refused every bottle her coach offered.
Only at the fourth cup, near noon, did the stranger read her instrument, smile, and leave.
rounds.chars: Chebet, an elite marathoner; Wanjiru (doping control officer)
rounds.story: Wanjiru was a doping control officer making an unannounced out-of-competition test in the 60-minute whereabouts slot Chebet had declared, so Chebet had to stay under her continuous observation, even while producing the sample. Under WADA's testing standard, a urine sample must reach a specific gravity of 1.005 on the officer's refractometer (1.003 if it is 150 mL or more), and since Chebet's pre-run hydration made her urine too dilute, each sample was sealed but more had to be collected until one passed, so she stopped drinking and gave up the run to stay in sight until the fourth was concentrated enough.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Chebet, an elite Kenyan distance runner training at a high-altitude camp in Iten.

**Character 2:** A doping control officer, who arrived for an unannounced out-of-competition urine test and had to watch every sample being given.

**Story:** Chebet had been drinking litres of water for her 40 km long run, so her first sample failed the officer's specific-gravity check with a refractometer: it was too dilute. Rules required it to be sealed anyway and the officer to stay for more samples. So Chebet skipped the run to stay with the officer and refused all water until her fourth cup near noon was concentrated enough, and the officer smiled and left.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A also explains the 5 a.m. knock through Chebet's declared 60-minute whereabouts slot, while Story B leaves the timing unexplained, so A accounts for more of the riddle's details.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

WADA's rules do require a minimum suitability specific gravity (1.005 by refractometer, or 1.003 by lab measurement) and continuous observation, but a sample that is too dilute is not sealed and kept: it is discarded, and further samples are collected until one meets the requirement, with only the final suitable sample being sent for analysis. The 1.003 threshold applies to a different measurement method and is not tied to a 150 mL volume, so the riddle's central mechanism of sealing every sample and the volume-based threshold is materially wrong.

rounds.riddle:
At a lavish wedding feast in Thrissur, the silk-clad groom lunged to swat a chilled cylinder from his father-in-law’s grip.
He hid it beneath his chair, trembling as an uninvited visitor methodically searched the dining hall's waste bins.
The visitor tasted no payasam, clutching only an official registry form against his chest.
If a single forbidden scrap was uncovered in the trash, the couple would be barred from boarding their midnight flight to Dubai.
rounds.chars: The groom; Health inspector
rounds.story: The official was conducting an unannounced Green Protocol audit, an environmental regulation in Kerala that strictly prohibits disposable water bottles and single-use plastics at wedding banquets. Under Kerala local governance procedures, the statutory Marriage Registration Certificate cannot be issued without the inspector's signed waste-compliance clearance, stalling the emergency spousal visa the bride required to board their flight that night.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** The groom, a newlywed Keralite about to fly to Dubai on a spouse visa.

**Character 2:** The local panchayat secretary, who is also the official Registrar of Marriages and an enforcer of Kerala's "Green Protocol" plastic ban.

**Story:** The secretary arrived with the marriage registration form and announced he would sign it only if the feast's waste bins held no banned single-use plastic. The groom knocked his father-in-law's chilled plastic water bottle away and hid it under his chair, because one plastic scrap in the trash would mean no marriage certificate, no spouse visa, and no midnight flight to Dubai.
rounds.judge:
B

Story B makes the visitor the panchayat secretary who is himself the Registrar of Marriages, so the registry form he clutches, his bin search, the swatted plastic bottle and the missed flight all follow directly. Story A needs a separate health inspector whose clearance oddly gates the marriage certificate.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

Kerala does have a Green Protocol for weddings and events that discourages single-use plastics, but marriage registration is not conditioned on a waste-compliance clearance from a health inspector, so the mechanism that stalls the certificate and visa is fabricated.

rounds.riddle:
When Callum tapped the hundred-gallon butt, the hollow ring betrayed that half the vintage was already gone.
Hearing Arthur descend the warehouse stairs with his brass measuring rod, Callum didn't grab sealant.
Instead, he shoved the heavy oak down the stone steps, shattering it directly across Arthur's boots.
Watching forty gallons of prime spirit wash the dirt, Callum smiled with relief as Arthur wrote a single zero.
rounds.chars: Callum; Arthur (excise officer)
rounds.story: A defective stave had secretly drained sixty gallons into the dunnage floor, creating a deficiency that far exceeded the statutory allowance for the angel's share. Under British excise regulations, an unapproved warehouse deficit incurs crippling back-duty unless certified as an "unavoidable accident," prompting Callum to deliberately stage the clumsy spill so Arthur would write off the entire barrel tax-free.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Callum, a bonded-warehouse keeper who had secretly siphoned off and sold half the cask's whisky without paying duty.

**Character 2:** Arthur, an excise officer (gauger) who measures casks with his brass dip-rod to calculate the tax owed.

**Story:** Callum knew that if Arthur gauged the half-empty butt, the missing spirit would expose his illegal sales and bring a crushing fine. So he "accidentally" smashed the cask on the stairs, because spirit destroyed by accident is duty-free and its original volume can't be proven, and a relieved Callum watched Arthur record zero gallons owed.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A's sixty-gallon leak leaves exactly the forty gallons that spill, and its accident write-off explains both the zero and Callum's relief, while Story B's "half siphoned" fits the forty-gallon detail less precisely.
rounds.fact:
REAL

UK excise rules for bonded warehouses do require duty to be paid on unexplained losses beyond allowed natural maturation loss, while losses from verified accidents can be remitted from duty (HMRC may remit duty on goods lost by accident), so staging an "accident" to explain an excess deficiency is a plausible fraud mechanism built on real rules.

rounds.riddle: At the Iten camp, before dawn, the pacer lined up with the runners but was told to stop at 30 kilometers, and he cried anyway. The champion later gave him half the prize, and the watch on his wrist was sealed in tape. A week afterward the champion's record was never ratified, yet the pacer's name was on the paperwork.
rounds.chars: Kiprop, a young runner from the Iten camp; Dr. Chebet, a World Athletics anti-doping official (doping control officer)
rounds.story: Kiprop, a pacer hired by the camp, had secretly been given an unlisted, banned iron-infusion drip by the camp's coach before the race, and he cried at 30 km because he knew his sample would expose the whole group. Under World Athletics rules, a record is ratified only if pacers who join mid-race are not used and every record-setting performance has doping control of the athlete, and under anti-doping rules a sample must be collected from the record-setter within hours; because the champion's sample was collected, sealed, and stored, but Kiprop was listed as an official pacer on the doping forms, the later positive result from his sealed sample (an A-sample, with the B-sample requiring the athlete's presence) invalidated the record by association, as the rules treat a pacer's violation as grounds to void a record made with his assistance.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Kiprono, the champion runner.

**Character 2:** Old Rotich, a professional pacer who is also the current record holder.

**Story:** Rotich wept at the start because he had been hired to help Kiprono erase his own record, and his watch was taped over to hide a rival sponsor's logo. Unable to abandon his protégé, he ignored the order to stop at 30 km and paced him all the way to the line, so Kiprono shared the prize with him. Because of that illegal full-distance pacing, the record was never ratified, and Rotich was named on the disqualification paperwork.
rounds.judge:
B
Story B explains every detail naturally: the tears over helping erase his own record, the tape covering a rival sponsor's logo, the shared prize for full-distance pacing, the illegal pacing voiding the record, and his name on the paperwork, while Story A rests on invented rules and leaves the taped watch and prize-sharing unexplained.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
Although record ratification does require doping control of the record-setter, and pacers must be declared, there is no World Athletics rule that voids a record because a pacer later tests positive, and the described A/B-sample mechanics and "invalidation by association" are fabricated.

rounds.riddle: Six relatives flew from Dubai to Kozhikode for Shahana's wedding. Each aunt wore one plain 40-gram gold chain and each uncle a 20-gram one, except cousin Niyas, who moved to Dubai only ten months ago and wore none. A man at the airport weighed every chain and waved them all through with a smile. By the next evening not one chain existed, yet the bride's father was delighted.
rounds.chars: Shahana's father Basheer; Rajeev (airport customs officer)
rounds.story: Basheer had bought all the gold for Shahana's wedding ornaments in Dubai and split it among the relatives, because India's baggage rules let a returning passenger bring gold duty-free only up to 40 g for a woman and 20 g for a man, so customs officer Rajeev weighed each chain, found it exactly within the limit, and had to pass it. That allowance applies only to someone who has lived abroad for more than a year and only to jewellery, not bars or coins, which is why ten-month resident Niyas carried nothing, why the gold was cast as plain chains, and why the family goldsmith could melt them all down the next day into the bride's wedding set.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Shahana's father

**Character 2:** A customs officer at Kozhikode airport

**Story:** Indian rules let travellers who have lived abroad for over a year bring in jewellery duty-free, up to 40 g for women and 20 g for men. So the customs officer weighed each chain, found it exactly at the limit, and smiled them through, while Niyas, short of a year, wore none. By the next evening a goldsmith had melted every chain into Shahana's wedding jewellery, and her father was delighted to have gathered her bridal gold without paying a rupee of duty.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A explains more of the riddle's odd details, including that the father bought and split the gold and that it was cast as plain chains because the allowance covers only jewellery, not bars or coins; Story B covers the same core idea but leaves these points unexplained.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED. India's baggage rules do allow duty-free gold jewellery for those who lived abroad over a year, but the limits are 20 g for a man and 40 g for a woman with a value cap of ₹50,000 for men and ₹1 lakh for women, and the allowance was not a plain exemption by weight alone; it applies to jewellery, and gold bars and coins are excluded, so that part is mostly accurate.

Correction: The mechanism is actually REAL.

REAL

India's baggage rules do allow duty-free gold jewellery for passengers returning after more than a year abroad, with limits of 20 g for men and 40 g for women (value-capped), and they exclude bars and coins.

rounds.riddle:
We pumped the heavy gray slurry down the steel vein to seal the porous bone,
The rubber dart struck home with a thud, and we killed the roaring pump.
Yet before a drop could spill, the fluid inside the pipe fell fifty feet in a breath,
The earth drank nothing, but the gray blood was fleeing down its own throat.
rounds.chars: Elias; Silas, the cementer
rounds.story: When the wiper plug bumped the float collar, the check valve failed to hold, triggering the U-tube effect where the heavy cement inside the casing dropped fifty feet to equalize hydrostatic pressure with the lighter mud in the annulus, returning fluid to the surface pits without losing any to the porous formation. To prevent the slurry from falling completely out of the casing shoe, the cementer immediately instructed Elias to apply wellhead holding pressure via the choke, counteracting the differential and trapping the gray blood in place.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Dale, the company man (drilling supervisor) on the rig.

**Character 2:** Rosa, a well-cementing engineer (cementer).

**Story:** Rosa pumped heavy cement down the steel casing to seal the porous rock, and the rubber wiper plug "bumped" its seat with a thud. When she shut down the pump, Dale panicked because the fluid level inside the pipe dropped fifty feet with no losses to the formation. Rosa explained it was just U-tubing: the heavy cement column was free-falling and pushing the lighter fluid until the pressures balanced. Nothing had leaked into the earth.
rounds.judge:
**A**

Story A explains why the cement could still fall after the plug bumped: the float valve failed, letting the heavy column U-tube back toward the lighter annulus mud. Story B treats it as ordinary U-tubing without saying how the column moved past a seated plug.
rounds.fact:
REAL
The U-tube effect after cementing is a genuine phenomenon: heavier cement in the casing and lighter fluid in the annulus create a hydrostatic imbalance, and if the float collar check valve fails, cement can flow back, so crews hold pressure on the casing (wellhead/cement head) to keep it in place. The details are slightly loose, since pressure would typically be held via the cement head or by closing in the casing rather than through the choke, but the mechanism is essentially sound.

rounds.riddle: Home of Champions, two thousand four hundred metres of thin air above Kerio — / yet the star trains only beneath the dying moon, / then stands, soaked and idle, at the shut gate from six to seven while his brothers churn the dust; / a stranger writes only his name, watches no stride, and leaves happy.
rounds.chars: the star of the Iten marathon camp; the stranger (Athletics Integrity Unit doping-control officer)
rounds.story: The stranger was an AIU doping-control officer on a no-notice whereabouts check: as a Registered Testing Pool athlete, the star must be findable during the one 60-minute daily window he himself nominates in ADAMS — he had chosen six-to-seven at the camp gate — so the officer's entire job that morning was to log a name, not watch a stride. Because the Code's obscure arithmetic makes any three whereabouts failures inside a rolling twelve months a two-year ban, identical in shame to a positive, and he already carried two strikes from a season of moving between camps, he ran his forty kilometres beneath the dying moon and stood soaked at the shut gate while his brothers churned the morning dust — which is why the man with the briefcase walked downhill happy.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Kipchoge-style marathon star training in Iten, Kenya's "Home of Champions" above the Kerio Valley.
**Character 2:** An anti-doping Doping Control Officer (occupation) on an unannounced visit.

**Story:** Because the star's mandatory "whereabouts" filing names a 60-minute window (6–7 a.m. at his camp gate) when testers may arrive unannounced, he runs his session in the pre-dawn darkness under the waning moon, then waits there, still sweat-soaked, while his training brothers do their morning run. The Doping Control Officer arrives, records his name and collects his sample without caring about his running at all, and leaves satisfied that he was present and tested clean.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A explains why the star is so anxious to be present at the gate (two prior whereabouts strikes away from a ban) and keeps the stranger's role to just logging his name, whereas Story B adds a sample collection the riddle doesn't support and gives no reason for such strict caution.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

The whereabouts system is real (three missed tests or filing failures within 12 months equal an anti-doping rule violation, with a 60-minute daily window entered in ADAMS), but the scenario has the mechanics materially wrong. Under the Code, the sanction for a whereabouts violation is normally two years, reducible to one year depending on fault, so it is not "identical to a positive". Also, a missed test happens when the athlete is not at the declared location during the window, so the officer's job is to attempt a test, not just "log a name". Finally, the story's logic is muddled: if the star ran his forty kilometres and was then at the gate in the window, he would not miss a test.

rounds.riddle:
At dawn he counts each breath on the dirt loop,
Last to scrape his ugali bowl, first on the physio table.
Tuesday fartlek he hugs the leaders' heels, never leading.
Sunday chai arrives: two cups steam, he touches neither.
rounds.chars: The breath-counting runner; the camp physiotherapist
rounds.story: The runner is a contracted pace-setter for the camp's three elite marathoners, logging sessions toward an agent's "development clause" that funds an international debut after 180 paced efforts where he must hold 180 strides per minute on dawn loops, counting breaths to cap his effort, and never lead Tuesday's fartlek. The agent's GPS auditor discards weeks where Tuesday lead-time exceeds forty percent, so he shadows the leaders, and he skips Sunday chai because the quarterly hematocrit panel requires a twelve-hour fast.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Kip, a young Kenyan distance runner.
**Character 2:** Mama Wanjiru, the training camp's physiotherapist and cook.

**Story:** Kip's twin brother, the camp's star, died last year, and Kip has vowed to break the course record only on the anniversary race. Until then he hides his fitness, counting breaths, eating slowly, sitting on Mama Wanjiru's table to protect his legs, and tucking behind the leaders, while every Sunday she pours chai for both twins and he leaves both cups untouched until he can toast his brother with a win.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A explains every detail with one premise: he hides his fitness for the anniversary race, and the two cups are for him and his dead twin. Story B relies on contrived contract rules and never explains why there are two cups.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

The scenario is a fabricated, highly specific contract mechanism (a "development clause" that funds an international debut after 180 paced efforts, with a GPS auditor discarding weeks where Tuesday lead-time exceeds 40%) that doesn't correspond to any real agent or athletics regulation. Also, hematocrit panels don't require a twelve-hour fast, and while pacemaking is real, the described structure is not a known real mechanism.

rounds.riddle: A cocker spaniel trotted through the bonded dunnage warehouse, sniffing at casks that had never leaked a drop. The gauger chalked the fresh-filled butt by the ventilator, and the distiller paled, though the bung was tight.
rounds.chars: Duncan Stewart; Ewan the Gauger
rounds.story: The gauger’s spaniel was trained to detect ethanol vapour escaping from stave joints. Under HMRC Notice 39, any leakage identified by an officer voids the standard 2% evaporation allowance, so the distiller would be charged duty on the entire three-gallon shortfall.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Biscuit, a cocker spaniel trained to sniff out spirit.

**Character 2:** Mr. Hale, an excise gauger.

**Story:** Biscuit wagged at every cask in the warehouse, since even the tightest oak lets out the "angel's share" of whisky vapour, but she walked straight past the fresh-filled butt by the ventilator because it gave off no smell at all. Hale chalked it for dipping, knowing a full cask that smells of nothing holds only water, and the distiller went pale because he had smuggled the real spirit out duty-free.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A accounts for every detail: sound casks still give off the angel's share, so the one silent, tight butt gives away the water swap, which is why the distiller pales. Story B relies on the dog detecting a leak, which contradicts the casks never leaking and the bung being tight, and it never explains why that particular butt was chalked.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

HMRC Notice 39 covers warehousing of duty-suspended spirits, but it contains no rule that an officer-detected leak (let alone one found by a sniffer spaniel) voids a "standard 2% evaporation allowance" and triggers duty on the whole shortfall; maturation losses are normally handled through allowances and loss-remission rules, not this mechanism.

rounds.riddle:
The copper serpent weeps clear fire into a locked glass cage,
But the crowned watcher halts the flow until the winter wind bites the brass.
He drops a floating glass eye into the stream to weigh the invisible ghost,
And if the liquid burns his fingertips, he taxes the phantom heat.
rounds.chars: Ewan; the Gauger
rounds.story: Ewan watches his clear new-make spirit flow through the copper lyne arm into the HMRC-locked spirit safe, where the government gauger intercepts the flow to measure the alcohol before it reaches the casks. Knowing the gauger’s glass hydrometer is calibrated for cold liquid and will sink deeper in hot distillate to falsely indicate a higher alcohol volume, Ewan must aggressively chill the boiling spirit with icy water to prevent the Crown from taxing the phantom alcohol created by mere thermal expansion.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Angus, a Highland whisky distiller.
**Character 2:** Mr. Pembroke, the Crown's excise officer (gauger).

**Story:** Angus's copper still trickled clear new-make spirit into the locked glass spirit safe, but Pembroke, who held the only key, stopped the run until the sample had cooled to the standard cold temperature of his brass instruments. He then floated his glass hydrometer in it to measure the strength of the "spirit." The stronger the burning liquor, the higher the duty he charged on its alcohol.
rounds.judge:
A

Story A explains the strangest line, "taxes the phantom heat," as the false extra alcohol reading a hydrometer gives in hot spirit, though it shifts the cooling from the watcher to the distiller, while Story B reduces that line to a plain "stronger liquor, higher duty."
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
Hydrometer readings are temperature-corrected (spirit is measured at 20°C with tables), and hot spirit actually reads as *lower* strength because it is less dense and the hydrometer sinks deeper, so it would not falsely raise the reading. Also, the spirit safe is not used to be chilled with icy water to dodge duty, and the lyne arm isn't a place where gaugers intercept the flow for such a trick.

rounds.riddle: A silent picket line parts for a flour-dusted man. / A gendarme checks a clipboard, then unlocks the door. / By noon, a tang of levain drifts out, but the strike sign still flutters. / A child tugs her sleeve: "Why does it smell of bread if they're on strike?"
rounds.chars: the flour-dusted man (a baker); a curious child
rounds.story: The baker was compelled by a judicial "mesure conservatoire" to feed the bakery's prized levain daily, so the gendarme verified the court order and let him in; the child realized that even during a strike, a sourdough starter is a protected intangible asset that must be kept alive to prevent its financial ruin.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Lucie, a curious little girl walking past with her mother.

**Character 2:** Henri, an elderly master baker and the bakery's appointed "keeper of the levain."

**Story:** The striking bakers and their bosses had signed a court-approved agreement allowing one person through the picket line each day, and the gendarme checked his list before letting Henri in to feed the bakery's century-old sourdough starter, which would die without care. No bread was baked or sold, so the strike held, but the sour tang of the living levain drifted into the street, and Lucie's mother explained, "They're not making bread, chérie, they're just keeping its heart alive for when the strike ends."
rounds.judge:
A

Story A naturally explains every detail (the agreed daily pass on the gendarme's list, the starter's smell without any baking, the strike still holding, and the child asking her mother), while Story B leans on a stilted legal premise and has the child improbably "realize" an abstract financial concept instead of asking the question.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

French law has "mesures conservatoires" (protective measures), but they are about securing a creditor's assets and are not court orders compelling a baker to feed a sourdough starter during a strike, and there is no legal category of "protected intangible asset" requiring a starter be kept alive.

rounds.riddle:
At first light the Iten mist swallows our stride,  
An old voice counts the beats of every heart.  
At mile twenty‑two my feet slam the wall,  
When the camp's bell rings six, the run must end.
rounds.chars: Moses; Samira (coach)
rounds.story: Moses finally faltered at mile 22, the classic glycogen wall that strikes most runners after 20‑plus miles at Iten’s 2,400 m altitude without a mid‑run carbohydrate boost. Samira reminded him that their sponsor’s clause forces every training to stop before the village’s 6 pm lights‑out, a little‑known effect of the town’s electricity‑saving ordinance that cuts generator power at sunset.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Kiprop, a young marathoner training in Iten, Kenya.

**Character 2:** Mzee Rotich, an elderly, blind running coach who "counts" each athlete's heartbeat by listening to their breathing and footfalls as they pass him in the fog.

**Story:** Every dawn, Rotich stands in the mist that hides everyone. Unable to see, he tracks each runner's effort by sound alone and calls out their pace, while Kiprop circles the camp's loop until mile twenty-two, where the route literally ends at the camp's stone wall and he slaps it with his feet to turn. At six o'clock the camp cook rings the breakfast bell, which is Rotich's signal that the session is over, because without sight he cannot read a watch.
rounds.judge:
B
Story B explains every line of the riddle: the dawn mist, the "old voice" as a blind elder counting heartbeats by sound, the mile‑22 wall, and the six o'clock camp bell. Story A skips the mist and the old voice, and it swaps the bell for an evening lights‑out rule that clashes with "first light."
rounds.fact:
INVENTED

The glycogen wall around miles 20-22 is real, but the central mechanism here is a made-up "electricity-saving ordinance" in Iten that cuts generator power at sunset and forces training to stop by 6 pm, and I know of no such law or sponsor-clause effect.

rounds.riddle:
At the stroke of eight the hearth sighs and dies,  
Yet the tatami still hums with lingering heat,  
The head of house watches, ladle untouched,  
And a rookie swallows the broth straight from the cauldron.
rounds.chars: Daichi; Matsuo (stablemaster)
rounds.story: Because a 1995 Tokyo fire ordinance forbids any open‑flame kitchen in a residential building from operating after 20:00, the Miyagino‑beya’s charcoal hearth is always put out at the stroke of eight, leaving the chankonabe to simmer on the iron pot. The pot’s lingering heat then radiates through the tatami and even warms the night‑time communal bath, so the oyakata never lifts a ladle while the fresh recruit drinks the broth straight from the cauldron.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** The Oyakata, a retired sumo champion who runs the stable and watches over its kitchen.

**Character 2:** Taro, a 16-year-old rookie sumo wrestler (the stable's lowest-ranked apprentice and chanko-nabe cook).

**Story:** By sumo-stable custom the senior wrestlers eat first, so by eight the fire is put out and the tatami is still warm from their heavy bodies having just lain there. The Oyakata, who had already eaten and does not need the ladle, watches approvingly as Taro, the lowest-ranked apprentice who must eat last and bulk up, tips the giant pot and drinks the leftover chanko broth straight from it.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A explains every detail naturally through sumo-stable eating order (fire out after the seniors eat, tatami warm from their bodies, the master already fed, the rookie drinking leftovers), while Story B rests on an invented fire ordinance and never really explains why the master watches or why the recruit drinks from the pot.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
There is no known 1995 Tokyo fire ordinance banning open-flame residential kitchens after 20:00, and a pot's residual heat wouldn't meaningfully warm tatami or a communal bath, so the described mechanism is fabricated.

rounds.riddle:
The thuds stop at 5:30.  
The elder eyes the clock, then the phone.  
At 6:00, the gate's bolt slides shut  
from the outside.
rounds.chars: a sumo apprentice; the oyakata (stablemaster)
rounds.story: The apprentice had been seriously injured during butsukari-geiko, and the elder knew the Japan Sumo Association requires an injury report within 30 minutes. Because the elder missed the deadline, the JSA's protocol automatically sent officials to lock the stable gate from outside, sealing everyone inside for investigation.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** Edna, an elderly widow with early dementia who tends to wander at night.

**Character 2:** Her grandson Sam, a carpenter.

**Story:** Sam spends each day hammering together a wheelchair ramp at Edna's house, stopping at 5:30 to pack his tools, while she watches the clock and the phone because he always promises to call once he's home. At 6:00, before driving off, he slides the gate's outer bolt shut as the family agreed, so that Edna can't slip out and get lost in the dark.
rounds.judge:
A
Story A explains every detail naturally (hammering thuds ending at 5:30, waiting by the clock and phone for his call, the bolt slid shut from outside to keep a wandering Edna safe), while Story B depends on an invented, implausible JSA lockdown protocol.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
The Japan Sumo Association has no known rule requiring an injury report within 30 minutes, and it has no protocol that automatically sends officials to lock a stable's gate and seal everyone inside for an investigation.

rounds.riddle: Lowest in a Tokyo stable, I cook the stew, wash the belts, and bow to men I may one day replace. Today the old man with silver shears reached for my topknot, but the master said: "Plain chonmage for him — no leaves." I bowed again and went back to stirring the pot.
rounds.chars: a junior sumo wrestler (the narrator); the stable's tokoyama (licensed sumo hairdresser)
rounds.story: The narrator is the newest, lowest-ranked wrestler in a Tokyo sumo stable, and by stable custom the junior man cooks the chanko-nabe stew and does the chores for his seniors. The old man with the shears is the stable's tokoyama — sumo's licensed hairdresser — and under Japan Sumo Association rank rules only sekitori (Juryō and above) may wear the oichō, the elaborate ginkgo-leaf-shaped topknot, so the master ordered a plain chonmage tied instead, since a lower-ranked wrestler's hair must not be styled with leaves.
rounds.solver:
**Character 1:** A young jonokuchi rikishi, the lowest-ranked wrestler in a Tokyo sumo stable, whose duties include cooking chanko-nabe and washing the senior wrestlers' mawashi belts.

**Character 2:** The stable's elderly *tokoyama*, the sumo hairdresser who dresses wrestlers' topknots.

**Story:** After the apprentice won his division's championship, the old tokoyama began to dress his hair in the ginkgo-leaf *ōichō-mage*, a style reserved for *sekitori* of jūryō rank and above. The stablemaster stopped him, since a lower-division title earns no promotion to that rank, so the humble apprentice kept his plain chonmage, bowed, and returned to stirring the chanko pot.
rounds.judge:
B

Story B explains why the tokoyama was about to tie the ginkgo-leaf ōichō at all (the lower-division championship) and why the master refused (the title brings no sekitori promotion), whereas Story A never explains why leaves were even considered.
rounds.fact:
INVENTED
The real rule (only sekitori, Juryō and above, wear the oichō in formal bouts and ceremonies, while lower ranks wear a plain chonmage) is accurate, and tokoyama are real sumo hairdressers who are Sumo Association employees, but the claim that the master "ordered" it as a matter of hair "not being styled with leaves" is a flourish rather than the mechanism, and lower-ranked wrestlers' hair is also typically done in a chonmage in daily life, so the central rank-based topknot rule works as described.

Correction: on reflection, the core mechanism is real.

REAL
Only sekitori (Juryō and above) wear the ginkgo-leaf oichō, lower ranks wear a plain chonmage, tokoyama are real sumo hairdressers, and junior wrestlers cook chanko and do chores.

rounds.riddle:
Five hundred banana leaves steamed under Thrissur's tallest pandal,
for the stars had fixed the muhurtham on the first of the month.
Gulf uncles landed with duty-free bottles, and one smiling uncle jingled the keys to the town's only licensed counter—
yet no shutters rose, no glass was poured, and every toast was sweet palada payasam.
rounds.chars: Devika, the bride; Sajan, a licensed bar owner (the groom's uncle)
rounds.story: The astrologer had fixed the muhurtham on the first of the month, the only auspicious day left that Chingam offered, so Gulf uncles flew in with duty-free bottles while the groom's uncle Sajan, a licensed bar owner, planned to open his counter for the wedding toast.
